utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today we are Monday, the 14th of January, 2008. I'd like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, and the accused. Today we must resume and proceed with our work. I have an oral decision to hand down, and I would also like to stipulate that as far as the upcoming witness is concerned the Prosecution will have two hours, that is part of the 92 ter procedure; and the Defence will have four hours. Each accused will have 40 minutes, which means all in all that would be four hours. As far as this witness is concerned this witness is to testify for a period of three days because this person has recently undergone surgery, he will only be able to testify for three hours each day, which means that we will have an hour and a half, then a break, then an hour and a half again, and we will stop after that. The same will apply for tomorrow and the day after. So that's how we're going to proceed. Now, as far as the oral decision is concerned, I shall read it out very slowly. Oral decision pertaining to the application of Rule 46(A)(i) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence re: Mr. Karnavas. At the hearing of 9th of January, 2008, Mr. Karnavas used an extremely offensive and intimidating tone vis-a-vis the witness. This attitude required a number of interventions on the part of the Bench to remind Mr. Karnavas that he was to remain calm and in control. Please refer to page 25964, 25965, and 25966. At the hearing of 10th of January, 2008, Mr. Karnavas, whilst saying that he was not asking to have one of the Judges of the Bench to be disqualified as is specified in Rule 15 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, complained about some of the questions that had been put by one of the Judges of the Bench which gave him the impression according to the words he used, re: Mr. Karnavas, that there is a fifth Prosecutor in the courtroom. Please refer to page 26045. Afterwards Mr. Karnavas stated that he was mindful of the concerns put to him by his client and was extremely concerned about the fair balance and legitimate judgement which his client was to be a subject of. So please refer to page 26046. The Trial Chamber notes that the behaviour of Mr. Karnavas vis-a-vis one of the witnesses as well as the words he used at the hearing when he compared one of the Judges of the Bench to a fifth Prosecutor with what such a comparison implies is unacceptable. This behaviour is offensive and obstructs the running of the proceedings pursuant to Rule 46 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. An order was handed down pertaining to the strict observation of order in the courtroom and confidentiality on the 17th of October, 2007. Mr. Karnavas has already been asked to comply formally pursuant to Rule 46(A) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Bench intervened on several occasions and asked him to remain or to have a respectful attitude during the hearing. Under such conditions the Trial Chamber feels that Rule 46(A)(i) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence should be applied. Consequently, the Trial Chamber has decided not to -- no longer hear Mr. Karnavas as of the 15th of January onwards and thus until the 24th [as interpreted] of January, 2008, included. It is only Mr. Karnavas's co-counsel, Mrs. Suzana Tomanovic, who will be able to take the floor at the hearing during this period of time. Mr. Karnavas will be entitled to be present during the proceedings if he abides by this decision and will therefore be able to follow the proceedings and communicate with his co-counsel. The Trial Chamber feels that the rights of the Defence of the accused Prlic have not been jeopardized pursuant to Rule 46(A)(i) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Registrar, you have the floor. Could you give us a few IC numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours. The list of documents tendered by Prlic Defence with Witness BF will become Exhibit IC 766. A list of documents tendered through Witness BF by Stojic Defence will become exhibit IC 767. List of Prosecution documents tendered through Witness BF will become Exhibit IC 768 under seal. The list of exhibits proposed by Defence for Milivoj Petkovic will become Exhibit IC 769. Slobodan Praljak's Defence list of exhibits tendered through Witness BF will become IC 770. Prosecution Exhibit list tendered for Witness EI will become Exhibit IC 771 under seal. And list of documents tendered by Defence for Mr. Coric through Witness EI will become Exhibit IC 772, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'd just like to make a correction. Regarding the decision that was handed down a while ago there's a mistake as far as the date is concerned. On page 3, line 9, it is not the 24th of January that you should be reading but the 21st of January. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, just wait a minute. You will have the floor. What would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First, I thank you for the decision. Second of all with respect to Judge Trechsel, as I indicated, it was my client who had that impression that it was Judge Trechsel that was asking questions every time a point that was scored for the Defence Judge Trechsel would then ask questions that it would appear were in favour for the Prosecution. That was the point. I also made the observation that I noticed it, and that has been a topic of discussions between myself and Dr. Prlic since the commencement of this trial. So I just want to make sure that the impression is correct, the impression, that is, that I left, that it was both myself and Dr. Prlic that felt that this was the case that on many occasions - and this is having looked at the entire transcript from the beginning all the way to this point where questions were being asked, but on that particular day we were quite concerned because the question was directed whether Dr. Prlic had actually or the HVO had invited the gentleman to come to Mostar when that wasn't the thrust of the question. But I accept the Court's decision. I acknowledge my own shortcomings, and I appreciate the Court's understanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I owe an answer to a Prosecution question with respect to the date when the programme was, or rather, when the video was filmed, broadcast, about the event in Guca Gora, and I said, I gave an answer previously, I answered questions where the video came from. I said it was from Croatian public tuition, that it was broadcast, and that Croatian television received this from an international exchange, that it was filmed by Terry Lloyd for the British programme the News at 10, and the second part was Martin Brand for Sky News, once again a British programme. However, I omitted to give the dates and that was part of the request made by the Prosecution. So with your permission I now have a that information, I have checked it out in your database and can tell you that the event itself in Guca Gora that is discussed there was on the 4th of June, 1993, that's when it took place, and that indubitably follows from document P 2849 and document P 2669. And there are other documents, too, which mention that same date, so I think that that is quite clear and not contestable. Now, as far as the filming is concerned, the British journalist or crew or cameramen were in Guca Gora with BritBat, and we can see that from the exhibit itself, they were there with UNPROFOR, that is, and according to the UNPROFOR document number P 2688, that took place on the 8th of June, 1993, so we must believe that that's when the material was filmed. And that material later on most probably, although I can't give you an exact date, but most probably it was broadcast over British broadcasting on the 11th or 12th of June when it was taken over by the Croatian television through the international exchange, and that is the regular mechanism that this is done. And it broadcast this same footage on Croatian television on the 11th or 12th of June. Now, if the Prosecutor wanted to ask about the authenticity of the material, I would like to remind you that at the beginning of the footage we can see the Croatian television journalist giving an introduction for the footage and it says that it was taken from the international exchange there, and we can provide evidence and proof of that. But if we begin discussing the authenticity of material like that, then of course the Defence would have a great deal of questions to raise with respect to Prosecution material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovacic, for having specified this. You have said that this pertains to events that occurred seemingly on the 4th of June, 1993. Yes. If I remember correctly, there was also another video which was shown at some other point which also shows Mujahedin inside the church of Guca Gora. And that video was probably shot after the 4th of June, 1993. I don't have a number to give you, but as I have a good memory it seems that there is a video that was shot after that date which would enable you to confirm what you have just said, that the event in question took place on the 4th of June, 1993, because the video which shows the Mujahedin in the church of Guca Gora was shot after the departure, which we can see in this video or people departing. So we all have ample opportunity to check this. Before bringing in the witness -- into the courtroom I believe that the Prosecution wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and greetings to all. The Trial Chamber's already addressed the issue which I wanted to raise, which was the scheduling for this witness's testimony, and so I have nothing to say at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So let's bring in the witness into the courtroom, please. Before the witness enters the courtroom I would like to tell the Prosecution that the statement which you are going to ask to tender into evidence also discusses other issues like the shelling of Sarajevo. So focus your question only by bearing in mind the indictment, so don't ask questions which are unrelated to the indictment, please. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, the plan is to -- I believe that Your Honours as well as the Defence should have in their binders numbered -- the witness statement which has been numbered. And we are actually only going to tender very specific parts of the witness statement as I think the last exhibit in the binder. We're only going to tender those very specific parts of the statement that relate to the items raised by the Trial Chamber in its decision requesting that the witness come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. So we are going to take the solemn declaration. If you'd like to stand up, do, otherwise if you prefer you may remain seated. If your health requires you to stay seated, please do. Very well, for the solemn declaration could you give us your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, my first name is Cedric and my surname is Thornberry and -- I'm sorry, what was the other question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My date of birth is the 22nd of June, 1936.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 36 or 26?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be a mistake then. In the statement we have it says 1926. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a consultant I think is the best way to describe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Monsieur, have you already testified before this Tribunal on the events that have unfolded in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, this is the first time that I have testified in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you take the solemn declaration, please..

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down. So just some very brief information I'd like to convey to you. As you know, you are, first of all, going to be answering questions which will be put to you by the Prosecution whom I'm sure you met over the weekend or this morning based on written statements which you have made a few years back. The Prosecutor will also show you a series of documents, after which Defence counsel, who are sitting on your left-hand side, will put questions to you as part of their cross-examination. The four Judges sitting before you can also at any time put questions to you. Technically speaking, it is better the Bench put their question after both parties have put their questions, but sometimes in face of -- on the face of a document or in light of a document it is better to deal with the issue straight away. We have been told that your health will not enable you to sit at this hearing for four and a half or five hours, so what we have decided to do, to make sure that you do not get too tired, is to have an hour and a half session, then we will have a 20-minute break, and then another session of an hour and a half, and then we will stop; and we will do the same today, tomorrow, and the day after. This is what we have planned to do, but if at any point in time you feel tired or if you wish to have a longer break please do not hesitate to let us know and to say to us that you would like to have a rest. So this depends on you. If you feel that you want to stop and have a break because you feel tired, do not hesitate to let the Bench know. Be as accurate as you possibly can when you answer the questions that are being put to you. If you don't understand the meaning of a question, do not hesitate to turn to the person who has put the question to rephrase it. The Bench is also there to answer any question you may have. This is what I had to say by way of introduction, and I shall now give the floor to Mr. Stringer, who will lead his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I just add for the record that the full 92 bis package for this witness is not in the binder and the matter of the mistake on the birth date is dealt with in the original 92 bis package which was originally submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you have -- I see I think you brought a binder with you in the courtroom today which was one that you were looking at this weekend; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And with your permission, I'm going to ask if the usher could actually take that one from you and give you the one that we want to use in the courtroom that's going to have the -- not have the stickers on it and the things that you may have placed on it. And, Witness, if I could ask you just to set that aside for a quick moment and I'm going to ask you questions about a number of the documents that are in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I begin asking the witness questions, I will provide this reference to the Rule 65 ter summary that we have for Mr. Thornberry. Witness Cedric Thornberry served as the director of civil affairs and later concurrently as the deputy chief of mission for the United Nations protective force, UNPROFOR, and the head of civil affairs as part of the United Nations mission in the former Yugoslavia. In the witness's perception the Serbs, and following closely in their shadow the Croats, were attempting to carve themselves out a large chunk of Bosnia-Herzegovina through ethnic cleansing. The idea that the Bosnian Croats were trying to carve out a piece of Bosnia for themselves was considered just a fact of life; it was not a notion anyone refuted. Around mid-August 1993 the witness travelled to Mostar and visited a hospital in West Mostar and met with HVO officials there. The witness indicates in his statement that during a meeting at that time it was implied that he would be killed if he attempted to visit East Mostar. On the 21st of August, 1993, the witness did enter East Mostar and spoke about the worst thing he had seen in the former Yugoslavia, with the exception of Vukovar, in terms of physical destruction. The witness will modify that statement and clarify it during the course of his testimony. On that day he visited the war hospital of East Mostar where the patients were kept in the basement. He saw wounded persons and amputees including children, people were sometimes three to a bed. A film crew was with him and television coverage of this was shown around the world. The publicity was intense and as a result the Croatian foreign minister, Mate Granic, met with the witness and subsequently said that he and Franjo Tudjman would put pressure on Mate Boban to allow humanitarian aid into Mostar. On the 25th of August, 1993, the witness was part of a humanitarian convoy that was bringing aid into Mostar. On the way to Mostar from Medjugorje demonstrating villagers blocked the convoy. A Bosnian Croat commander had to stand on the APC and tell them all to get out of the way. The witness will also modify and clarify that part of his witness statement as well. The convoy entered East Mostar and unloaded humanitarian aid. When the convoy was to leave, residents blocked the convoy. The people were scared that if the convoy left the HVO would continue to bombard the area. The convoy stayed in East Mostar until the 28th of August, 1993. The people in East Mostar were living in very difficult conditions and it was the witness's impression that civilians were just as much a target of attack as the military. According to the witness, snipers had gone out of their way to attack those through whom they could extract the most morale. Bosnian Croats desperately wanted Mostar as their capital as they saw it as the heart of their state. On major issues such as Mostar, the witness believes it was the Croatian leadership and not the Bosnian Croats who were calling the shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, with that, Witness, let me ask you to take the binder that's in front of you and turn to the last document at the end of it which has been marked with a tab, Exhibit P 10041, P 10041, it's the very last document in the binder, I believe.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Excuse me, did you say 10041?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you could just turn that page that's in your hand, that's the exhibit in front of you.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And with that in front of you, let me just ask you a series of questions about that document. Looking at the first page do you see your signature?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is this the witness statement that you provided to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor in May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, but we covered some of this ground in 1999 and updated it more recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then if I could ask you to just turn through the statement. Your initials appear on the bottom of each of the pages and then does your signature appear again at the very end of the document? You don't have to look at each page. If you could just perhaps in general indicate whether your initials appear on it and then your signature's at the end?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm those elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, as you've indicated, the statement covers a great many topics, and my question is whether at the time you provided this statement, you answered the questions of the investigator truthfully?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I believe I certainly did answer them truthfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you answer the questions freely? Was there any coercion involved or were you providing the statement voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I do not remember whether there was any coercion, but I don't believe there was. I was used to sometimes quite difficult circumstances when working for the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then after your arrival here in The Hague just within the last few days, did you have an opportunity to review this statement, and in particular the specific portions of the statement that you and I discussed over the course of the weekend?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And were you given an opportunity then to make any corrections or modifications to those parts of the witness statement that we discussed?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I remember what the timing was, but I think that we changed the date of my birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then over the weekend --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, I'll propose perhaps as we go into the statement I could take the witness to the specific parts that he had comments on because it's a rather large statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In general, Witness, the parts of the statement that you and I discussed - and if you recall, I can direct you to them - and for everyone's information paragraphs 1 and 5 which relate to your personal history, that's on page 2, that section there. And then turning to page 11, page 11, paragraph 42 is a one-paragraph section under the heading of "the warring factions' intentions towards Bosnia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Not yet, sir -- yes, I find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then just continuing on, skipping until page 14, under the heading: "Conflict between the Bosnian Muslims and the Croats" --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- which has paragraph number 54 written next to it. Do you see that? It's handwritten.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I see -- which paragraph did you ask, please?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: And this is on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is under the heading: "Conflict between the" --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And then just continuing from that point across to page 15, 16, 17 in which you're talking about your time in Mostar during August of 1993, and then to page 18, which continues down until the next section on Srebrenica, do you see paragraph 72 there?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Those sections there that we've -- I've just taken you to, subject to the modifications that we will discuss, if I were to ask you questions and if you were to give this statement again would your answers be the same? Would your information be the same as that contained in these parts of this witness statement?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I'm certainly not -- I certainly have nothing to say which would directly controvert what is here, but there may be changes in shading I think is the best way for me to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll be talking about these -- a number of parts about this. And so if you see something that you'd like to address in terms of shading, you inform me --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- and you'll be free to do that. Witness, I'm going to just briefly direct you to paragraph 2 of the -- of this statement which relates to your background and your experience, both before you joined the UN and during your time with the United Nations --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I see one of the accused is on his feet, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hadn't seen Mr. Praljak. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we don't have the paragraphs in our translation which will make it difficult to introduce the mistakes, or rather, corrections. So could the Prosecutor tell us what the contents are because our copy isn't numbered, the paragraphs aren't numbered, and it will be difficult to compare the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in fact, in the B/C/S translation I see pages but I don't see paragraph numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, as we always have to do with these witness statements, Mr. President, we have to write in the paragraph numbers by hand, which we've done on the English. It was my assumption that counsel could have done that for the B/C/S versions, but it's my -- it's my intention to take the witness to the specific parts of the witness statement. So I don't think there will be any trouble for the accused to follow along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since there must be a corresponding page you can see paragraph 42 and page 11, and this corresponds, for instance, to the fourth and fifth paragraph on page X in B/C/S. Maybe you can proceed this way so that Mr. Praljak can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The other alternative, Mr. President, would be to take a break so that counsel could number it since the Prosecution did not number. This is not something that we should be doing, it is their evidence. I think the only I think that's fair to Mr. Praljak and to the others is to take a break so we can just go ahead and number it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, what do you think of this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think I can continue, Your Honour, and we'll just do our best to refer the accused to the B/C/S version. There really isn't that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before we actually turn to some of the parts for modification, I wanted to just briefly highlight your experience within the United Nations system which is indicated on page 2 of your statement, page 2. And particularly in paragraph 4 on page 2 of the English version there is a reference that from March of 1992 until March of 1994 you were the director of civil affairs for the UNPROFOR. And from August of 1992 you also served as the deputy chief of mission for UNPROFOR. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I do. There are -- is a slight complication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Why don't you go ahead and address that at this time then.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: It has to do with the United Nations names for various functions. I was, in fact, a director of administration and management for the whole of the United Nations worldwide for a fairly short period of time, and then I would have reverted to my internal statement, I think is the best way to try to describe it. So there were two series of administrations - I'm sorry about this - but there were two series of jobs -- job contents; and from time to time I had fulfilled one and at another time I filled another. I doubt whether this is, if I may say so, if this is material, but I thought again I had to try and maintain the absolute accuracy of that remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. Before we get deeper into your statement, I just wanted to ask you briefly whether in your capacity on behalf of UNPROFOR and civil affairs, whether it was customary for you to receive reports from your subordinates who were working for you in various other locations?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, I received numerous reports more or less daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. If I could ask you to turn to a different document that's in the binder, which is Exhibit P 01353.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to be clear, this is more of the 92 ter phase of it now because I'm going just a little bit beyond the scope of Mostar, but it's going to be a very brief reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, it's one of the first documents in the binder. The usher might need to help you locate it, P 01353.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise that document, any of the names on it?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I think all the names are within my knowledge. If you asked me whether I remembered everything that is in that cable, then I would have to say: No, I cannot do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is this a report that you received from a Victor Andreev?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: It appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then, regarding the info, there is the name "Santana." Is that another name that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: That is the name of Aracelly Santana, a United Nations staff member, who was fulfilling the task on assignment as political affairs officer in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now it appears that this document is from January 1993. Is this the type of report generally that you received from people like Mr. Andreev during the time of your tenure with the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I'm sure it wouldn't surprise anyone if I said that there were many different ways in which my colleagues would have reported to me, and certainly Andreev was one of the most assiduous and detailed in his analyses and sending them to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In this document there's a reference to the map. It says that --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- referring to the HVO, and I'm in paragraph 1 on the first page.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "They are always quick to assert and announce territories of the 'map' which are under their control." Do you know which map that's a reference to or what this is about?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: First, no, I don't know what it's a reference to; but second, I have an awareness -- I had an awareness at that stage of -- I'm sorry, I'm just looking again at this document. I think the content of the statement is fairly accurately set out in the paragraph below that which states one political -- and Andreev was one of our best, most experienced reporters, rapporteur I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. If I could ask you to set aside that document, and I'm going to refer you to now the time that you talk about your trip to Mostar which occurred in August of 1993. And again going back to -- in fact I don't know if the usher might be able to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It might be faster if we could remove the witness's statement from the binder because I'm going to be asking him to move back and forth between the statement itself and then specific documents which are in it, it's the very last document, 10140.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, now, Mr. Thornberry, if I could ask you to turn to what we've marked as paragraph 56 which is found on page 15 of the statement. The statement is the other document outside the binder.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't follow what you were saying about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You know, I'm going to ask, Mr. President, the usher could stay with the witness. I think it would move things along to assist the witness in navigating the various documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, please stay next to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So this is paragraph [sic] 15 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I have paragraph 56 in front of me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm told that this is page 11 of the B/C/S version. Now, Mr. Thornberry, paragraph 56 is sort of the beginning of your trip to Mostar. In August of 1993 you indicate that you were in Split and then came to Medjugorje and then began your meetings there and other activities that you're going to be talking about. In the binder I want to ask you to go to Exhibit P 03858. And I'm going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you for and for counsel I'm going to direct the witness to the press release for the 19th of August, 1993, which is with the ERN number ending with 9705.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That should be the very first document in front of you there. Okay. Mr. Thornberry, just starting at the bottom of that, do you recognise the name there, Shannon Boyd, who that was?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: She was the acting spokesperson for the UN, for UNPROFOR, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And does this appear -- was it part of her job to accompany you and to issue press releases about the events that were taking place?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: It was often part of her job to do that, but it was relatively unusual for a spokesperson to go to the field rather than staying back at home base and developing their awareness, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the third paragraph of this document there is a reference to meetings which occurred on this day. Your name is mentioned, Mr. Andreev is mentioned, members of the Spanish Battalion as well. And then on the HVO side a Mr. Zubak, Mr. Stojic, and a General Tole. And it's indicated here that on this day also you and others went to visit the hospital which was on the west side of Mostar. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, I see that in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of the technical booth I'm going to ask that -- actually, maybe then I do this by myself. I'm going to play a very short video clip and ask if you can comment on that for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "MR. THORNBERRY: Well, I think it's more than a gesture. I think the most important thing that UNPROFOR could do in this area is to do everything possible to have Mostar opened up to humanitarian aid. This city has been undergoing siege and conflict for a very long time. The amount of suffering which is immense here is absolutely unacceptable, and the international community must have an opportunity of bringing in humanitarian aid and helping with its good offices to resolve this local conflict."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, you're shown there in the clip. I wonder if you could tell the Trial Chamber about this trip to the hospital in West Mostar, how it came about, if you recall at this point.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: First of all, I still -- I still agree with what I was saying there ten years ago. Secondly, as shown in the binder, we were met -- we were caught cold someone said by the information we were given when we came to Medjugorje from Split. We didn't expect anything like that to happen. I had no indication that it would happen. However, we sat down and with a number of colleagues from the political side of the UN, and we went into this and discussed it at length, took information from other people, and began to prepare for a possible and previously unthought-of mission to Mostar itself, West Mostar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I hope that -- I hope I made that clear. I will try otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll ask you a couple of follow-up questions on that. Who was representing the UNPROFOR civil affairs in the Mostar region at that time?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: We had two colleagues who were there at that time, Mr. Albert, I've forgotten his second name for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: And another guy called Ed Joseph. These were two principal actors on the ground. Both of them were assigned to the Medjugorje office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as indicated in the press release there that we looked at, there are indications there that you had meetings with various HVO officials on the 19th of April. Do you recall that meeting at this point, what was said or ...?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I must say quite frankly that after ten years or 11 years, it's very difficult for me to recall individuals and to -- yeah, to recall individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I should correct the record, Mr. President, I asked about the 9th of April, apparently, and I intended to ask about the 9th of August --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: 19th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 19th of August. Thank you. Witness, then is it fair to say that in general terms you don't have a specific recollection of meetings that took place during this period of time in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: That's broadly true, but I do have memories of discussions between ourselves and the other side, and we also discussed in detail shortly after Mr. Granic began to appear on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you about Mr. Granic a little bit later. We're still looking at paragraph 56 of your witness statement, and in that paragraph you state that: "Although the HVO officials we met with did not say this directly, the gist of their response was that they would kill us if we attempted to enter east Mostar." So I should ask you, Mr. Thornberry, then what you can say about that statement at this point, given that, as you've indicated, you don't recall specific meetings with specific individuals.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, in my time peacekeeping for the United Nations in which I perhaps appeared in 15-odd different locations, I was threatened with death with some regularity. It usually meant that the other side was beginning to, as it were, scrape the barrel for their -- a part of it was part of an argument. It may have been true, I didn't take it seriously, I have to be quite blunt about it. I thought it was part of a point in a -- a part of a point in a negotiation. I hope that doesn't sound too flippant, but as I say people quite often when they were driven into a corner did react in a way which was maybe exaggerated and which we wouldn't necessarily have paid much attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did -- was the HVO during this very initial part of your trip to Mostar, do you recall whether the HVO in general was supportive or not supportive of efforts to get humanitarian aid into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, the thing is, you see, sir, that the HVO together with everybody else who was in Medjugorje at that time, was a part of the negotiation, a continuing negotiation. And as I said before, I think that that is the basis on which we received their evidence, their statements. They were not to be disregarded, but they were also not necessarily to be given higher worth than they might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could ask you to turn the page of the exhibit that's in front of you, the press release of -- because we put them in specific order in that binder for you. I'm going to ask that you refer now to the press release for the 20th of August, 1993, and this is with the ERN number ending in 9704 for counsel. Now, Mr. Thornberry, this press release makes reference to another meeting held in Medjugorje at the Spanish Battalion on the 20th of August, 1993, meetings with yourself; the SpaBat commander, General Morales; General Milivoj Petkovic, HVO commander; Mr. Bruno Stojic, president of the HVO defence department. And on this point I want to now show you another video clip which is a brief one which is called Thornberry clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, apart from yourself, Mr. Thornberry, was there anyone else in the video that you're able to recall or identify at this point?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I can recall a number of them, but I cannot identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. I think I heard you mention the name Shannon Boyd there at the earlier part of it?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Shannon was the press and information acting chief, an American woman who was normally working for the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, but who was in effect in secondment to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Does this appear to be video footage of the meetings that were held on this day, the 20th of August?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Certainly so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could ask you then to turn again in the binder to the next document, which is marked as 9495. Now, Mr. Thornberry, we -- you spoke a little bit already about some of the reports coming to you, so let me ask you briefly to describe who it was that you were reporting to.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: That was a big question because we had recently changed the special representative, and I don't know whether this -- I think this document related to communication with the new incoming former High Commissioner for Refugees, Thorvald Stoltenberg, and he was the person to whom I normally reported, however, as you will have seen from the documents, the reporting chain was a very complicated one, which certainly I will go into if you wish, but I'm not sure that they would add a lot of information. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is this a report that you then prepared and sent to Mr. Stoltenberg, Kofi Annan, and others?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly Stoltenberg and probably Andreev as well as Ms. Boyd.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise your signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And does this relate to in paragraph 1 meetings held on the 20th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. It indicates there: "Meetings here today with Stojic and Petkovic of HVO ..."

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's indicated here that they had: "... Agreed to facilitate humanitarian relief convoy Saturday to the Muslim side ..."

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: That is what I think this shows, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: If I might just add to my answer. I see also that Lieutenant-General Briquemont was also -- I also reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then Hayes was a general at the UNPROFOR headquarters --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: He was a brigadier-general, British army, reporting to Kiseljak and to -- and to other senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if I could take you back to the press release of the 20th of August, which is Exhibit 3858, because in this press release Shannon Boyd is attributing some quotes to you, and I wanted to ask you if you could comment on those. I'm looking at the fourth paragraph in which you state that: "We have expressed to both parties our determined intent to open routes for humanitarian supplies, freedom of movement for UNPROFOR, not only in Mostar but throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then continuing you say: "'Our urgent concern is to have the humanitarian relief programme, which will be required whatever the outcome of the current Geneva negotiations, fully operational before the onset of winter.'" Could I ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stringer, to interrupt you. I do not find in that document which you refer to Exhibit 3858. Is it in the same exhibit what you are quoting now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, it's in 38 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: -- 58, yes, but there are a number of papers in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, if you look at the bottom right-hand corner there are some numbers that are stamped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if you turn to the one that is stamped 00079704, 9704.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, thank you very much, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, one of the issues, actually, that the Trial Chamber has invited you to give evidence about is the issue of humanitarian aid and access to humanitarian aid. And just keying off of this press release and the quotes that are attributed to you there, could I ask you to address that issue, humanitarian aid, how significant was it to you at this time?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I'm very happy to try to answer that question because it was an extremely important issue for us. The provision of humanitarian aid was one of the major tasks -- in fact, it was the major task of the -- of UNPROFOR, both within Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the mission area as a whole. And during the time when I think which is most relevant, perhaps from the middle of June and for the next -- certainly the next six weeks was that we were beginning to obtain -- we were given reports, given reports, by our offices in different parts of the country and by the military, who were particularly important on this. And they brought to our attention, essentially to my boss who was Mr. Cot, they brought to our attention the fact that because of interference with the relief columns which was being undertaken -- so far as I could identify, by everybody in that part of the world at that time, I say "everybody," I mean by the various military forces were beginning to use aid, humanitarian aid and medical aid, were using that as part of a negotiation. And this was beginning to bite very hard, indeed, on the situation, the humanitarian situation, humanitarian obligations of the -- of the UN military. So putting it very -- as briefly as I can, this was beginning to be the -- certainly the most important consideration on the part of the UN and the part of UNPROFOR. And we were trying -- we for our part were trying to find ways around the blockades and the -- the blockades which were being run at that time by a number of countries' military, and especially by the -- those who were working in Bosnia. Bosnia was absolutely critical, and I remember one of our generals telling me that if something was not done to break this blockade, that the "spectre of famine," I remember him saying, the "spectre of famine will be all over your country, all over your land, if this is not done." I'm sorry to be so long-winded about this, but it was a very significant thing that was said to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was this an issue that was part of the negotiations in Mostar, particularly in respect of East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yeah, it was very much in the forefront of our preoccupation. We had to break that blockade some way or another, preferably, preferably, by negotiation. The UN on the whole does things by negotiation. We are not a war-making entity; we are a peace force. And that can sometimes be misunderstood, but that is usually the most effective way in any event of bringing home to the countries as a whole, the various countries, the best way of relieving some of the suffering which was being felt by people all over the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, if you would turn the page to the next press release which is for the 21st of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for everyone else, this is the page -- it's in a different part of the exhibit. It's with the stamped numbers ending 9696 continuing to 9697.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in this press release Shannon Boyd is writing about a trip that you made with others to the Muslim area of Mostar on the left bank of the Neretva River. And while I ask you or before I ask you to talk more about this -- the information in this press release, perhaps we could just take a look at the next video, the last video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "MR. THORNBERRY: We have to establish some kind of stable route, wherever that comes from, Croat side, Serb side, to get access to this area."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, is that footage then of the trip that you made into East Mostar on the 21st of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: What were the dates again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 21st of August, that was the press release that we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if it's time for the break yet or when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall have a break now. It is just about 20 to. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, the hearing is resumed for another hour and a half. The witness will be able to rest afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, just before the break we had looked at video footage of the trip into East Mostar, the -- and in a few minutes I'm going to ask you about a second trip that you made into East Mostar a few days later. But at this point my question is to ask you to inform the Trial Chamber, give some general comments on the humanitarian situation as it existed in East Mostar on those two occasions in August of 1993 when you were present there, the humanitarian condition of the population in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: The situation of the population of East Mostar was, it appeared to me - and I was also told - was very much worse than that in West Mostar. It was evident that people and especially children were undergoing great physical difficulty. One of the problems was that children seemed to be targeted quite often by unidentified snipers. Moreover, the condition of adults in that side of the town seemed on visible -- on apparent view to be quite difficult and to involve the beginnings of -- serious beginnings of lack of nourishment, food, the danger of shrapnel from bombs and -- and the general condition was very poor and apparently getting worse according to our Spanish Battalion APCs who until a little earlier had been running into and out of Mostar. If you have any specific question about that, I would be glad to try to answer. It was a very widespread problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a question, sir. I heard very carefully what you just told us, and I remembered the video clip that we saw a couple of minutes ago. I was thinking of these children in Mostar east that were going to get water, some of them were carrying canisters of water or jerrycans. Two things hit me. As I was watching the video, I was able to notice that these children all seemed to be in perfect health and I was able to also see that they had water and that everybody was walking around with jerrycans of water, and I also noticed that people are walking quickly. They do not give the impression of being exhausted as if they had eaten well. So when I listened to you, you're talking about snipers, shooting, so on and so forth, but I am under the impression that a few things are being confused here. One, the population and their survival in terms of everyday life and the difficulty they had in terms of nourishment and so on and so forth. We've been hearing witnesses for two years now in this trial. We've received also listings of humanitarian convoys, not one, two, or ten, but hundreds of humanitarian convoys. We saw lists of convoys leaving from Zagreb going to all sorts of places in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, a Judge listening to what was going on and a Judge that likes to wonder, to think, to ask himself questions, and I belong to that category of Judges, I do not take everything at face value, I'm just wondering what is the reality of this health situation? Many of your international colleagues testified, and I put these questions to them already, I asked already if somebody died of hunger but nobody told me, Yes, people died from starvation. So what is the real, exact situation, could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, thank you for that question, and I appreciate your consideration of that matter. I also noticed in the video, in the blow-up of the video, that the children and young people by and large, by and large, looked fairly healthy. Some of them were playing in the street, and they had there evidently not been totally -- their morale had not been seriously affected. One saw this very much indeed with the children playing around the armoured personnel carriers of the Spaniards and otherwise. I am not a doctor. I have no way of making an evaluation of the health of children living in -- under such conditions, and I was very much aware of that when we were in Mostar particularly on the first visit we made to Mostar. We also had a great deal of contact with the doctors, the surgeons and doctors there and also in an area which I'm sure will be referred to Nova Bila, which was a church turned more or less into a hospital. I'm afraid I do not -- I cannot answer that question. Perhaps it might require evidence which I don't have, but I had absolutely no doubt in my mind, having seen in particular children in a hospital room, in a hospital bed, with two other children. When I saw them with amputated limbs looking cheerful into the camera, I thought that there was something seriously wrong. My final point, however, is this: I don't think I have been trying to say, I have been trying to take this in a dispassionate manner. It's difficult with kids, but I have been -- I have been under no doubt that what the doctors were saying to us about the condition of the population and of the children in particular, that they were -- the problem -- I'm sorry, let me say -- let me re-say that. What we were particularly being briefed about was the condition which was beginning to fall upon cities such as Mostar, towns and villages throughout the country. It was not yet in many cases a reality, but it was a threat, a major threat, as testified to us by two in any event of the physicians or surgeons in that part of Mostar. I hope I have given some assistance on this matter, sir, but I cannot be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have a great deal of experience. Your personal history shows us that you went to Namibia in various parts of the world which were in trouble, and you were able to compare, I suppose, places where we see people suffering from starvation and that live under terrible conditions such as Darfur, for instance. But from what you were able to see in your own experience, what you saw in East Mostar, is there something that you would like to insist on, to tell us. Do you -- can you make a comparison? Would you like to highlight something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of my experience has been in the Middle East, and there the problem was shelling rather than famine. Is it possible for me to think about that for a moment -- for a little while, perhaps to come back to it? I should like to be of assistance to the Court in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you wish, sir. Since you are here for a couple of hours you will be able to go back on that answer. But talking about 1993, if I remember correctly, in Somalia there were also problems, famine problems and starvation problems, et cetera. Would you -- were you able to compare what was going on in Somalia and Mostar, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when you went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, both -- the children in both parts of the city in -- I was in Somalia for a fairly short time, about six weeks actually, and I travelled a little bit but not a very great deal into the areas in which there were reported to have been famine conditions. I didn't see those conditions in Somalia, probably because I wasn't there long enough nor was I able to move too far around the countryside for a variety of reasons. I find it difficult to go beyond saying that the unambiguous and -- the unambiguous evidence in Mostar was very much more daunting than anything I saw in Somalia. But if I might think better on that because, as I said, my -- I was also stimulated by what I saw of that film clip, and there were a number of -- a number -- it was a very revealing document I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will get back to it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, you had pointed out that my last question was somewhat general, and let me try to make it a little more specific on this issue of the humanitarian situation in East Mostar. Could you address specific items such as shelter and the structures as they existed in East Mostar, water, and then thirdly the situation that you found in the hospital on the east side of Mostar, those three points, perhaps starting with the issue of shelter and the physical structures in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I'll try. I think I mentioned that there did not appear to be any single building in East Mostar which had not been affected by gun-fire. Usually shells, mortars. Sometimes in using anti-aircraft shelling for -- as ground strafing. I'm not a military man, I don't know what the definition of it is, but if there were very many different forms of attack on the population which were actually taking place. As regards water, we were told by the medical persons who were -- who had remained in Mostar, East Mostar, that the population was obliged to rely upon water from the river, which was heavily polluted and apparently contained many indications of entero -- I'm afraid I can't remember the word exactly, but in effect it was some kind of stomach illness coming from using polluted water. One of the concerns was that typhoid was -- had to be very close by. That's one, two -- sorry. Could you mention to me again the third aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The hospital --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- when you visited the hospital in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, the hospital was truly dramatic or melodramatic perhaps in its -- the manner in which the patients were being treated. My understanding was - and again evidently this is coming to me from other people, not my own direct perception - the condition of the hospitals without electricity, without adequate water, without any of the other major life-giving and life-preserving elements. Blood, for example, one can go through a list of items, many of which were either in shortage or were not, in fact, available at all. I think those are the three major items, but perhaps there might be others which -- to which one can speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We are essentially talking about paragraph 57 of your witness statement, and this contains one of the modifications or additions that I believe you'd indicated you wanted to make. Yeah, this is your witness statement on page 15. If the usher could assist you, perhaps. Page 15, the second full paragraph where you --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You indicated that: "On entering East Mostar," you "were confronted with a situation worse than anything I've ever seen in Yugoslavia with the exception of Vukovar." And the statement reads "in terms of physical destruction," and I believe you had a modification or something you wanted to add to that, the last term of that sentence in terms of the physical destruction.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: This is paragraph 57?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, it says that: "We visited the hospital, a building converted for the purpose and found most of the patients in the basement, the safest place. There we found many wounded amputees including children, sometimes three to a bed."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In that paragraph did you want to indicate also that you found human and physical destruction?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may say this before the witness answers. I did not object so far, but my learned friend from the Prosecution went beyond the allowed scope with his question several times. This does not change anything to the meaning, at least until the Prosecutor puts words into the mouth of the witness. This is obviously a leading question. The witness read the question, said he had nothing to add, and nothing should be added by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, do not put words in the witness's mouth; in other words, don't ask him to add something, to add something as to his written statement. You can say, for instance, in paragraph 57 you said this: "Do you confirm what you said," for instance. I'm not quite convinced of what Mr. Kovacic just said, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm just trying to bring the witness to a few of the modifications he had previously indicated he wishes to make now, but I won't suggest to the witness again what those would be if he doesn't have anything to say today about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the witness said something to the Prosecution during proofing, then they should have taken the trouble of making a new statement that the witness would have signed if that was supposed to be led as evidence. We have nothing in writing, the witness did not confirm it, I suggest that the Prosecutor move on. It is a fine point in any case, but as a matter of principle I cannot agree that leading questions be allowed to go so far because the next time the same thing will be done on a question which is critical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me summarize. In paragraph 57 you described a hospital in East Mostar, then you describe the city in a general way. Do you have something to modify as to the way you described things in paragraph 57 or would you like to maintain that paragraph without any modification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no modification in mind and nothing has been brought to my attention this afternoon to persuade me that a modification should be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, turning to paragraph 60 of your statement, you indicate that by the 23rd of August there was intense media coverage of your trip into East Mostar and the conditions that prevailed there at the time. And then at paragraph 61 you make a reference to a Mr. Eide of the International Conference for the former Yugoslavia and yourself as having been called by the Croatian foreign minister, Mr. Mate Granic. My question is whether you met Mr. Granic in Zagreb then as a result of this contact?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Granic indicate a willingness to assist you in organizing a convoy into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: He did indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Granic then subsequently came to Mostar himself?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: He came to Mostar, I met him in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, please, based on your observations to what extent during this time did Mr. Granic -- to what extent, if any, did Mr. Granic have influence over the control of decisions that were being made about Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, there are two parts of an answer to that question. First of all, Mr. Granic was the foreign minister and he told us, he told me in any event, that he had been -- he had spent some time with his president, Mr. Tudjman, the previous day looking at this situation of convoys of military decisions that were having substantial humanitarian implications and so on. And he said that his president, President Tudjman, now deceased I'm sorry to say, Mr. Tudjman had told Mr. Granic that he, Tudjman, thoroughly supported his position in regard to the movement of convoys and of their content of humanitarian goods and medical goods. So in other words, he had given -- he had given his full support said Mr. Granic, to what Granic was actually doing; that is to say, behaving in a manner that was perhaps very impressive from a humanitarian point of view but would have been rather an unusual position to take up in regard to a democratic government where ministers are usually expected to tow the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then the other part of my question was: Based on your observation, the extent, if any, to which Mr. Granic was able to exercise influence or control over the decisions about Mostar.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't think that he went to Mostar or certainly not at that time, but I do believe that he had, as he told us, discussed with his president the previous evening, in other words, the evening of the day when we had been to east and West Mostar, rather, not very fully in some cases -- I'm sorry, I can't remember what the other part of your question was on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me direct you to paragraph 63 --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- of your statement and you talk about: "On ... Wednesday, the 25th of August," just as you were ready to leave, "Mr. Boban and Mr. Granic came to see us for an hour," and you go on to talk about that. And so again my question is whether Mr. Granic had authority or influence over the decisions that were being made about Mostar.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: First of all, I should say that I noticed only today at lunchtime the fact that in paragraph 63 there is a very serious error. It states that -- paragraph states that -- let me see. 63, it -- the statement appears to say: "This was an aggressive self-righteous, face-saving visit ... for the benefit of the press." I think some of those adjectives are inaccurate, and I'm sorry that I had failed to pick them up on the first time they went around. I would not say those things at the moment with consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me -- and I'll bring you back to that --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: With respect, I'm still hoping to get an answer to the original question which was whether based on your observations Mr. Granic could exert influence or authority about Mostar.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, he did -- I'm sorry that I haven't made myself clear on that, I should have done. I thought I had, actually, made this fairly clear. Mr. Granic is foreign minister was -- I think he still is foreign minister, and the next sentence is gratuitous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Apart from what you say in the statement, Mr. Thornberry, do you have a recollection now based on your observations at the time what was happening?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Granic able to exert control or influence over the Bosnian Croat authorities whom you were meeting with during this period?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, without any doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you elaborate in what way -- what's the basis of that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: What Mr. Granic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: He said that he was able to get hold of Boban and that Mr. Boban would find himself obliged to do as Mr. Granic had requested. He also said, however, that it wouldn't require much influence because Mr. Granic was ready to -- either to modify his statement or to withdraw it altogether. Does that answer your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And then the final series -- I was going to say it's the final series of questions but it's not quite but we're almost done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I apologise. On the English channel we're hearing your question in French, so I don't -- and nothing's been interpreted up to this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me start from the beginning. What I was saying, on reading your written statement we have a clear impression that in Zagreb because of the media coverage in the area, this is in paragraph 60, you explain that all of this has been publicised in Mostar, the British, the Americans, the Germans are all there, all the television crews are there. And it seems that Tudjman and Granic do something in favour of humanitarian aid that is to be brought to Mostar. Now, you discuss matters with Mr. Granic and Mr. Granic tells you that he is able to convince Boban re: The decisions that have been taken. And you tell us that in paragraph 63 there's a mistake because one is under the impression that Boban and Granic had an aggressive attitude to this. No, this is not what I meant. So a Judge in Tuzla [as interpreted] wonders whether there has been a humanitarian convoy that left from Zagreb with the political approval of Mr. Granic and Mr. Tudjman. And the local authorities, amongst others Mr. Boban and perhaps other people, made sure that the humanitarian aid convoy could move forward. Is this how you experienced things when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One moment, please, sir, while I read this. Yes. Thank you. I don't think that there's any question that Boban and Granic had an aggressive attitude. I don't know what happened in private between the two of them. I know that Granic came down to Medjugorje in order to create a different and better situation to the one that had been put forward before. I'm not sure I understand what is meant by the reference to a judge in Tuzla. And then finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tuzla shouldn't be mentioned here. Nobody ever mentioned Tuzla. In the transcript we can read Tuzla; that's got nothing to do here with what's being said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So does that mean I don't need to make any comment on that? Because I have a comment to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The aggressive attitude of Boban and Granic, are we to understand that both men were not in agreement and that there was some dispute or disagreement between the two men? What do you have to say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I try to answer your question, sir. It is a mistake for me -- it would have been a mistake for me to have had the political approval of Mr. Granic and Mr. Tudjman. I think that is probably true. The word "aggressive" is the one that I object to. I don't think that was the atmosphere which we had, and in any event it is very difficult, sir, if I may say so, to enter into this in detail because presumably the parties would close the curtains, as it were, and be unwilling to discuss what happened between a prime minister -- president and his foreign minister. I would certainly be surprised if that issue was left open. I don't think Granic adopted an attitude of aggressiveness. I think he probably explained to Mr. Boban - and this is supposition, sir - I suppose he would have expected to state to Mr. Boban and others that it was time for him to finish and exit from this issue which was otherwise important, because we do find other references later to Granic's continuing shall we say "liberal" position vis-a-vis his own government and his own president. It was a very unusual action, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you're saying sounds very complicated. It's difficult for me to understand. So it's either one or other situation. Either Mr. Granic explains to Mr. Boban that things have been decided and that there will be a humanitarian aid convoy and Boban has to accept this and has his back to the wall, or Mr. Boban is shuffling his feet and does not agree with the decision that has been taken. So as you were in contact with all these people, the decision that was taken to send the humanitarian convoy, did this not give rise to any difficulty; and if it did give rise to any difficulties, why did it and at what level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Boban was probably overruled by his president, which is something that I do not find surprising, but which perhaps in the circumstances was rather conclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Thornberry, to whom do you refer when you say Boban and "his president"? Who would be the president of Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tudjman I think would be the president of Mr. Granic. Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Here you spoke of Mr. Boban. Did you mean Granic rather than Boban? Line 7 of page 46 you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Line 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- "Mr. Boban was probably overruled by his president." Did you say "Boban" when you were thinking of Granic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I was thinking of Boban. Mr. Boban was hierarchically subject to the authority of the president evidently, but I think was also less -- had less authority than Mr. Boban did.
