utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an unusual situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber what according to your recollection the position of Mr. Boban was formally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was the head of government of the Bosnian -- the Bosnian authorities. He was -- he had the responsibility, the authority, to deal with those authorities and to, as we see perhaps in this occasion, to present this issue to his president, Mr. Tudjman, and to say to Mr. Tudjman, I have talked now to Mr. Boban and he sees that he could or should follow the line which I am -- I am taking. Sorry if I'm using a lot of words. I suspect I'm making this much more complicated than it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me for having interrupted you, President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You seem to say that Mr. Boban was a subordinate of Mr. Tudjman in your mind. Mr. Boban has a president above him, and that's Mr. Tudjman. That's what you seem to be saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But question, in that case Mr. Tudjman is president of the state which is called the Republic of Croatia; Mr. Boban is a citizen of another country which is called Bosnia and Herzegovina. So how do you establish a connection between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding, sir, is that the situation in that part of the world was a very complicated one with different authorities and different capacities. This is the only way to be able to explain Mr. Tudjman's attitude and the attitude of Mr. Boban and these are the facts of life in that particular part of the world at that particular time. As I say, it is irregular to anyone who has a clear or determined adherence to the rules of democracy or of parliamentary democracy. We don't have a parliamentary democracy situation here, but we do have clearly different sources of authority. That's what I'm trying to say. I'm not sure that it's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we have understood what you have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Still I would like to return to this paragraph 63. Frankly, I do not know what you are saying now. You have said a bit vaguely that you withdrew some objectives that you would not put in anymore, but are you still saying that the visit Messrs. Boban and Granic paid to you or paid to East Mostar was a gratuitous act, a show, a [French spoken] for the press, or do you take that back and accept that they visited this because it was an area of problems, and they had responsibility and took their responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would certainly endorse the second point of view that you mentioned, sir. What I found in this paragraph when I read it regretfully for the first time today was use of language which I would not have -- I would not have deployed. It is too crass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, just one follow-up question on this point that the Judges have been asking you about. I'm looking at the transcript at the top of page 47 which you were asked what, according to your recollection, was the position of Mr. Boban formally. And you said: "I think he was head of the government of the Bosnian authorities." This is in the transcript, Mr. Thornberry, it's not in the statement. It's just a follow-up to one of the responses that you just gave. So my question -- you had indicated that: "He was head of the government of the Bosnian -- the Bosnian authorities." My question is whether you can provide any more specificity there. Was there any particular element within the Bosnian authorities that he was in charge of or head of?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I'm not sure that I can go beyond what I've actually said in paragraph [sic] 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I know what he himself described himself as, and that was the head of the authorities. I think we -- I think we have correspondence with him which actually confirms that, but I -- to be very frank, I don't know that I can go behind what I think he actually stated to us. It didn't -- what it did do was to place the responsibility on Mr. Granic and Mr. Granic was the main, the principal, actor in this situation I suppose with the UN that they were undoubtedly in charge of the event. Provided that, let me again be blunt, provided that the generals who were under his authority complied with decisions which Mr. Boban and Mr. Granic took. That is another question and perhaps it's one of some interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- I'm going to shift gears now because we're just sort of starting to touch upon the issue of the convoy of 25 August 1993, and I'm not going to ask you to go into the details of the convoy as they are set out in your statement. But there is one clarification I'd like to ask you about. On page 16 of your statement at the bottom, paragraph 65 --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do you mean the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yeah, perhaps the usher could assist you with turning to page 16, paragraph 65 of the report --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Got it, thanks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- where you indicate that the convoy was finally underway and it comprised about 50 trucks. And then the statement continues to the next page where you indicate that: "Within a mile we were halted for an hour by demonstrating women." You make reference to a Mr. Stojic there and then continuing you make reference to Citluk and a Bosnian Croat commander. I wonder if you could just tell the Trial Chamber, please, what you recall now about the incident or incidents referred to in this paragraph in which the convoy was stopped and then was allowed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, that was what happened indeed. The convoy set off from Medjugorje at perhaps around 1600 hours in the afternoon, perhaps 1600 hours in the afternoon, but when it reached to Citluk the -- it seemed as if an organized demonstration was taking place on the part of the villagers and that demonstration was against us and it was intended apparently to prevent us from moving forward and instead holding us -- keeping us still. I don't exactly know why it would be speculative for me to enter into that particular decision. I am not sure, and though I was there, what Mr. Stojic -- who he was and what he was doing at that point. I was imprecise in my knowledge of the local authorities in Bosnia at that time. I wasn't very much involved with the events of that kind except in regard to the convoy and to some other actions. The villagers began to throw stones at the convoys, and the military -- my military colleagues, the Colonel Morales and others were becoming quite nervous - well, so was I - as to what was going to happen next. In fact, after about an hour, as I remember it, maybe an hour and a half, a Bosnian officer came from the houses around Citluk, the main street through Citluk, and leapt up on the bonnet of an APC, I think it was an APC, it might have been a regular vehicle, a command vehicle for the convoy, I don't remember that exactly. But they climbed up on the -- or he climbed up on the truck. The crowd applauded him and said, Good for you, sort of thing, but they did disband and we proceeded to the airport where we were apparently going to have to spend the night because we were very late and it was already dark. I don't think I can remember very much more about it than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification. You indicate that a Bosnian officer emerged, and we have to be more specific about whether you're talking about a Bosnian Croat or a Bosnian Muslim or a Bosnian Serb. You've indicated that -- this in paragraph 65 of your statement, but if you could specify.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I believe he was a Bosnian Croat, senior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall as you sit here today who that was, who the person was that came and spoke to the crowd?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: And if I were to suggest otherwise, it would be pure speculation I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You've touched on this briefly already, but I know that it's something that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Witness, please. If the person who climbed on the vehicle was in this room, were in this room, would you recognise him? If the person who jumped on the bonnet were in this room, would you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I doubt it. I think probably not, not more than 20 per cent chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 69 of your statement which is on page 17, you've touched on this already, but I'd like to ask you to address this specifically, the issue of sniping. In this paragraph you talk about sniping and your impression that the civilians were equally targeted. My question is to ask you to tell the Trial Chamber what you saw yourself and what you experienced in relation to sniping in East Mostar and on what basis you form your views about sniping as set out in paragraph 69.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I wasn't hit by a -- strike -- a sniper and I didn't, in fact, see any incident involving sniping. However, the military on whose expertise I was throughout dependent, warned me of certain areas in Mostar into which I should not venture other than under armour. And I was told by them to beware of these areas, and if I did enter into them I might very well be injured or -- at best. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When you say the military --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- could you specify which military.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I mean the colonel and captains and senior officers of the -- of the military presence who were giving -- who were driving us and giving us advice. They told me that if I did cross these areas safely, it would be remarkable and they said, Well, if you are by any chance left out for any reason, if on some -- in regard to some action or another you are being left out or if you are talking to radio broadcasting somewhere in the west -- western Europe, that I should try to take evasive action as we moved along. There was a phrase used that has remained in my mind and that was the reference to Sarajevo a hundred or so kilometres away and the phrase used was: The Sarajevo sprint, the Sarajevo sprint, that is to say running at full pelt, head down in a zigzag format, the Sarajevo sprint.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: It was not apparently completely successful because it was apparently the main -- the main problem there was in terms of small arms and bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry, my last exhibit is in the binder at 4673, if you could turn to 4673. Do you recognise your signature on this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: This is my document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's a report from the 1st of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: That sounds quite plausible. I don't remember the date, but that sounds right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you see the date there under your signature?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there's a reference in your statement to the Nova Bila hospital, and my question is simply whether after then the convoy went into East Mostar, did you subsequently travel to the hospital that was at Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And paragraph 2 of your report here indicates that you're heading back to Zagreb. So does the 1st of September then essentially bring to a close your involvement or your direct involvement in these events in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: No, because the -- it led to a new chapter, as it were, in this horrifying story. Nova Bila was a church its congregation is not -- was not a congregation but a -- but it was a series of the -- in the body of the church the pews had been pulled together so that they lay alongside one another and the patients lay on those wooden pews. I had an involvement in visiting, as I had pledged to do, in visiting Nova Bila, but once I got there it was a very interesting and revealing, though still horrifying, location. And after that, the lead-on after that was -- and it was, I thought, in a way the most important thing that I had to do there was because the underlying object was to try to get the parties to agree to a new basis of relationship at that time; namely, to take, with their agreement of course, children and adults to safe havens, I would use that phrase I think, in various adjacent parts of the country, i.e., Bosnia-Herzegovina and also, I think, Croatia. And these -- the -- it was necessary in my opinion and in the opinion of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees and also of the International Committee of the Red Cross, all of whom I consulted on the matter, and the outcome of this was the beginning of a new air-lift to remove people from -- patients seriously wounded or sick patients, to have them removed from that area to other areas which were, in fact, safe and which had medicaments and which had medical staff to deal with these. So that my action was after that began. My direct involvement continued after that began but very difficult -- very quickly afterwards other problems cropped up in regard to that Nova Bila location.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then were you ultimately able to achieve some medical evacuations, both from Nova Bila and the hospital in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thornberry, for your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have some follow-up questions. When we look at your written statement that also talks about different topics, I noticed that you met many political figures of the region, Izetbegovic, Milosevic, Mladic, Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As well as some other political figures. Now, what I would like to know is I would like you to tell us something about Tudjman and Boban. When did you or how many times did you meet Tudjman, to begin with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 20, maybe, 25 times. I'm not too sure about that, might be more, might be a little bit less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And what about Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Boban I met only perhaps four, five times. I understood later that he was quite unwell and he has, indeed, passed away in the meantime. But I didn't know him well at all because -- essentially because I didn't have very much involvement with the -- the fine print, as it were, of the relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993 your main office, where was it, was it in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our main office was technically in -- no, no, it was in Zagreb. We had, however, a further, and both military and civilian office, at Kiseljak to the west I think of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You yourself went to Bosnia and Herzegovina on few occasions. I saw that you went to Vitez, you went to Mostar. During that period, how much time did you spend on the ground, how many days to speak your terminology, to use your terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My goodness, that's difficult to remember that off the top of my head. I will commit myself, however, and say perhaps two-thirds -- perhaps three-fifths of my time was spent outside Zagreb usually dealing with matters coming to me from other areas that were -- with other areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I didn't have any further questions for you. It is ten past 5.00. I was told that we have to finish the hearing of today at 5.32, so we would have some time left. Would the Defence like to finish their cross-examination or wait until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll start, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you have until 5.32. If you are not done, since you have 40 minutes, your colleague will finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Picking up where his President -- the President left off, in looking at your statement as I understand it you were in country more or less for approximately two years, March 1992 until March 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Maybe February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: February --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: February of 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But more or less -- up -- approximately two years?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And looking again at your statement, it would appear that at least initially your primary focus had to do with Security Council Resolution 743 that dealt primarily with Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I certainly dealt with mostly Croatian issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And when we're talking about the Croatian issues, we're talking about as a result of the JNA attack, situation that was happening in the Krajina, that's what we're talking about, correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, not only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: We also have to look at the situation in the sectors, all of which had different consequences --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: -- none of which were good news.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say "consequences," you're referring to, for instance, humanitarian issues, refugee issues?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, also the practice of expulsion of populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you say "expulsion," who was -- is this by the Serbs expelling Croats or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Both of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it's -- it says over here in your paragraph number 8 you say that initially the assessment by the colleagues in New York was for you folks to put your headquarters or to have a basis in Sarajevo because it would be invidious to have headquarters in either Zagreb or Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I apologise for the interruption. I'm looking at the Trial Chamber's decision on bringing this witness here which laid down limitations on both direct and cross-examination, and it appears to me that this question goes beyond the scope of the Trial Chamber's ruling on cross-examination. I say that only because I limited my direct in an attempt to conform to the Trial Chamber's decision, and I believe that counsel should be held to the same limitations that we've adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was under the impression that the Trial Chamber was seeking the truth. If I mistook that impression, then fine, I'll move on. But I don't see how I can possibly jump into something without laying a foundation. The reason for that is this: At some point, as we all know, the move out of Sarajevo, it's my understanding, and they're located in other places, but he uses the word invidious, and I wanted to know why invidious. Was that because you wanted to demonstrate impartiality, was that the purpose?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please. To give an answer to Mr. Stringer's objection. The decision that had been handed down on 15 November 2007, I would like to read it out to you, it's paragraph 54. It's a very long decision but this is what was said: "The cross-examination has to be limited to the subjects or the topics which are relevant when it comes to the indictment with regard to the municipality of Mostar, including its mission to Mostar from mid-August 1993, the restrictions to the access of international and humanitarian organization to Mostar east in the month of August 1993, the sniping on the population of Mostar east, the control exercised on the Republic of Croatia regarding all the decisions relating to Mostar, as well as the meeting on the 19th of August, 1993, with official representatives of the HVO." This is what we had set out in that decision. These are the limits. Maybe your question is part of those limits, but once again maybe you should reiterate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase Your Honour, I'll rephrase. I don't wish to have my time taken up with preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 39, sir, this may assist the Trial Chamber, I hope it does. It says: "Personally I did not pay significant attention to Bosnia-Herzegovina until the beginning of 1993 having to focus on the issues within Croatia which as I saw more political." So at least from paragraph 39 it would appear from 1992 that you were there. It wasn't until sometime in 1993 that you actually began focusing a little bit on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, that was me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're speaking about you, sir, we're not speaking about somebody else.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: We had approximately 15 general officers in our area of responsibility, and that meant that we had the ample opportunity of demarcating, of identifying people as against particular functions, one of the functions which I was given was to try and get a Joint Commission to look at the whole question of both -- the whole question of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But again -- and I don't mean to be disrespectful, but I'm not speaking -- I don't have 15 other people here I'm cross-examining, I have you and I'm going through your statement. So that's what I'm trying to cross-examine you on your statement because we're here to seek your knowledge, whatever you have.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: By all means I shall try to facilitate you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, sir. Now, you say that at one point, and this was brought out on direct so I think it's safe enough for me to go into it on cross, on paragraph 42 you indicated or it was indicated that you said: "My perception was that the Serbs and following closely in the shadow of the Croats were attempting to carve themselves out a large chunk of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then if we go to paragraph 55 you say that: "The idea that the Bosnian Croats were trying to carve out a piece of Bosnia themselves was considered just a fact of life. It was not a notion anyone refuted." My question to you, sir, is: Since you were there since 1992 in March, were you aware of any of the international negotiations that were going on and any of the particular plans, such as the Cutileiro Plan? Were you specifically aware of the contents and what was being pushed actually by the international community?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I was aware of a number of attempts to gain -- to gain peace, to achieve peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if the Cutileiro Plan, for instance, called for three regions, would it be Mr. Cutileiro who was actually trying to carve out Bosnia and Herzegovina so that the three constituent peoples would each have their own region within a sort of weaker state the way it ended up with the Dayton accords? Would you characterize Mr. Cutileiro as trying to carve up Bosnia and Herzegovina, yes, no, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, and I apologise for the interruption. This is beyond the scope of the Trial Chamber's ruling on the scope of cross-examination. I've limited my direct, and I think it's unfair to not hold counsel to the same limitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wish to be heard. I wish to be heard and make my record, Mr. President. I understand that the Trial Chamber may think otherwise, but you did allow the gentleman to go into this paragraph. He mentioned that -- in fact, it was Mr. Stringer himself that read out the summary and paraphrased. So now I'm going back and I am questioning him about the very same issues that were raised by the Prosecution. So how is it that I'm going beyond the scope? If this is going beyond the scope then I should sit down because obviously the Trial Chamber does not wish for me to conduct a cross-examination. This is part of -- this is a response. The same thing goes on re-direct. Re-direct is limited to what comes out on cross. So it's the same principle that's being applied here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And Mr. Stringer, Mr. Karnavas says that while summarizing you mentioned in a certain way the topic that he is raising now, so he believes that during his cross-examination he can come back to what you mentioned in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've stated my objection and I'll clearly accept any decision the Trial Chamber gives on this question, but I think it's worth bearing in mind that there are limitations have been placed that I viewed applied to me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If that were the case, Your Honour, I presume the limitations were [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please put your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... If limitations were imposed and he knew those limitations, why did he go into them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your question, Mr. Karnavas. Since the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Going back to --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- The Cutileiro Plan ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Going back to paragraph 55, you go on to say: "Saying this, I was almost completely bogged down in Croatia and did not really focus on Bosnia -- on Bosnian issues. Now, I mentioned this so maybe this might assist you in answering the previous question, and I'm asking you concretely now. Could you please tell us what exactly was the Cutileiro Plan since you were in country at the time or shortly thereafter? What did it envisage and what were the respective positions, if you know. If you don't know, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I don't think I know. I don't think anyone merely because of their presence in UNPROFOR knew what was happening. The Cutileiro Plan fell within the ambit of the European community, not of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, while you were there doing whatever you were supposed to be doing and because of all the things that were happening you were not keeping track what was happening in Geneva with the negotiators?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, I was, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: At that stage -- let me be precise, please. What date are you talking about because that's important in the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I was going to get -- my next question is so then we go to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. So surely now you're going to tell me the exact details of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and perhaps you can explain to us where in the Vance-Owen -- what did the Vance-Owen Peace Plan call for and how does that jive, how do you reconcile that with your bold statement that the Croats were trying to carve out a piece of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Nobody challenged that; that was the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, sir? Could you please tell us what were the basics of it. And you need not look at the Prosecution. He cannot help you.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I'm looking to see whether anyone is going to say anything to you about this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To object?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: -- because I don't know what the detail of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was, it hasn't been publicised. By the time this document comes into -- becomes implemented, only then does one begin to know what is going on in the Vance-Owen, Stoltenberg, and the number of -- there were a different layers of negotiation. This is very untidy, especially for lawyers, but this is the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Untidy in the sense that it's pretty complicated and convoluted and not everybody has the answers?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, that's part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it's fluid situation, would that be correct? Fluid in the sense that things are moving along and pretty difficult to know at any given moment what is happening?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes, but that's is the job of a political operation, especially of a peacekeeping operation, is to keep track of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you went to Mostar, you went to East Mostar and you were asked specific questions again, I think it's within my right of cross-examination, you talked about shelters, physical structures, and water in East Mostar. My question, first of all: Do you know what was happening in Mostar in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did anybody explain to you that in 1992 Mostar was shelled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I knew that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You knew that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did anybody explain to you or show you for comparison purposes which structures had been damaged by the Serbs versus which structures were being damaged now by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Did they have a little flag on them you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I'm not being facetious nor flip, sir. I'm asking you because you went there and you went around with the media and there's a purpose why I'm asking this question because you went around with the media and you wanted to bring out attention and you indicated that not since Vukovar had you see anything of the sort. And I'm asking you did anybody point out to you, because obviously you were totally unaware of the destruction and havoc that had been suffered by Mostar, but did anybody actually point out to you in East Mostar what the Serbs had done so you could say, Okay, now I know the extent of the Croats what they're trying to do, did anybody point that out to you?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: That's a very good point and the answer is no I don't think anyone gave me an overall picture, they gave me partial pictures -- pictures of particular areas of destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, very briefly. We saw the video not long ago, we see streets on that video, we see buildings with some holes on the walls, and the question that Mr. Karnavas is asking you is the following and I asked myself that same question when I looked at the video. How could somebody know what happened -- how can somebody make a distinction between what was caused by the Serbs and what was caused by the Croats and the Muslims. The question is an excellent one, since that is also the question that I asked myself. You were in a city. Combats took place in that city with the Serbs as well, so how can you, you are an authority of course, how can you make the distinction as to who did what to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to think about that for a while because indeed the condition of the city was appalling when we entered it. Our Spanish friends, our colleagues who did a great deal of the ground work, they pointed out to me and to others when they were -- when their task was to brief us, they told us what area and amount of devastation had been -- had taken place, but they said, This is only partial, this is only limited. That's the best I can do, I'm afraid, sir. I can't re-write history on that subject or at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were asked again about Nova Bila. I'm just touching --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- a little bit. My colleague will finish up on the cross tomorrow. But -- now this was, I take it, your first time in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry, I beg your pardon. I think I made a visit to Vitez at one point but there were very few visits on my part to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But as I understand it your visit to Vitez had I think taken place around August of 1993 if I'm not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: A little bit earlier than that. I can't remember exactly either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll find it here in a second but in any event: Now you say in your statement that this was a media circus, and this caught my eye, and I noticed that before you corrected yourself you said it was crass, that was the word that you used, in the way someone, whoever wrote this statement out for you to sign, put those words down there for you to adopt. But was it your intention to adopt this phrase, that this was -- or this sentence that this was also a media circus?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: No, it certainly wasn't any part of my intent to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it the situation as you say: "My impression of Nova Bila was that while it was not quite like Mostar it was still grim, impoverished and unhygienic."

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Sorry, please could you say that again because I think I missed out on something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Paragraph 70 you say: "My impression of Nova Bila was that while it was not quite like Mostar, it was still grim, impoverished and unhygienic -- improvised" I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Improvised, yes I'm sorry. I've got it here "improvised and unhygienic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You stand by that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Otherwise it says the things that are in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The situation was pretty bad?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: It was pretty bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that for the Bosnian Croats, that was a concern, that essentially the other side, the Bosnian Muslims, were allowing this situation to occur, and this is why your assistance was being sought, to alleviate this situation?

utterances.speaker: CEDRIC THORNBERRY
utterances.text: Well, it was to make it possible for people to return and live in peace in their own hometown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I think that that's all I have for right now. We reserve the rest of our time for tomorrow in keeping with your earlier ruling my colleague -- and just I don't know if we have -- I hope we'll have 30 seconds I would like to say something on the record, Your Honour, but outside the witness's presence. I don't think it's necessary for the witness to hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You will be able to rest now. The hearing is adjourned. Tomorrow we will resume your hearing at quarter past 2.00, so you will have to come tomorrow at 2.15 p.m. and you are kindly requested not to have any contact with the Prosecution until then. I would like to ask Mr. Usher to accompany you to the door.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before I give the floor to Mr. Karnavas there for a few seconds, I would like to read out two oral decisions which are urgent and which need to be handed down. One of them will be read out in open session and the other one in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The oral decision to be read out in open session relating to the 98 bis procedure. The hearing of the 10th of January, 2008, the Prosecution asked the Chamber to ask the Defence to file a skeleton of its arguments that it will present orally pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Defence teams objected to this. The Trial Chamber recalls that Rule 98 bis of the Rules was amended to shorten the procedure. Thus, the arguments of both parties and the decision of the Chamber are from now onwards handed down orally. As far as these three decisions pertaining to the Scheduling Order is concerned, the Trial Chamber has clearly reminded the parties that the arguments presented pursuant to Rule 98 bis can only be presented orally, and the Trial Chamber will not allow any written submissions to be made on that count. The Prosecution has submitted no arguments that would justify this decision to be re-examined. Therefore, the Trial Chamber dismisses the motion filed by the Prosecution. I would like now to move into private session so I can read out the second decision.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to end the day by making sure that no one left here with any misunderstandings. It is with great humility that I accept the Trial Chamber's decision concerning Rule 46(A)(i), that's number one. Number two, I will endeavour in the future to rectify any shortcomings, and I do take on board the Trial Chamber's observations. It was never my intention to offend anyone. In fact, I should say not in my defence but just by way of an explanation at the end of the cross, I did exchange pleasantries with the witness, but I do fully understand the Trial Chamber's concerns and it certainly was not my intention at any point in time to offend Judge Trechsel, nor do I wish to leave the impression that either I or Dr. Prlic in any way are concerned that at the end of the day we will -- any member of the Bench will do anything less than their level best to ensure that everybody receives a fair trial, that's not just the accused but also the Prosecution. And again my deepest apologies to Judge Trechsel if, indeed, I have offended you, that was not my intention. And again, I will endeavour in the future to work on my shortcomings, and thank you for being gracious enough to point them out to me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas for your kind words. As far as I'm concerned, what I would like in 2008 is for the hearings to unfold in the best atmosphere possible. The purpose of the Bench is to try to understand what has happened during these years, 1992, 1993, based on evidence which both parties develop, the Prosecution and the Defence. The Trial Chamber have to see through what is being presented without there being any drama, any unrest. What we are only interested in is seeking the truth, whatever the truth may be. So I'm fully aware of the fact that everybody will do their best to make sure that we have a pleasant atmosphere in the courtroom and that each and everyone, if we are as we are in an adversarial system, that each and everyone can answer the question, put the question, cross-examine, and raise any uncertainties or doubts that he or she may have. And it is with that in mind that I am fully convinced that everybody will tow the line this year and I think -- I am sure that this trial will unfold in the best conditions possible. The trial has been ongoing for two years now already, and we might still be together for the next two years because if the Defence has the same time as the Prosecution this is what will happen. So let's all try to make sure that all of this unfolds in the best possible atmosphere. I wish you a nice evening, for, as you know, we shall resume tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00.
